lesson.title: Complex Numbers: A New Kind of Number for a New Kind of Problem
lesson.summary: Introduces complex numbers, the imaginary unit j, and the rectangular/polar forms and arithmetic you need before circuits with sinusoidal signals can be analyzed.
lesson.body:
Ordinary real numbers can describe a lot, but they run into trouble with an equation as simple as x squared equals negative one ,  no real number, positive or negative, squares to a negative result. Mathematicians solved this by inventing a new number, usually called i, defined so that i squared equals negative one. In circuits you will use this same idea constantly, but engineers write it as j instead of i, purely to avoid confusing it with the symbol for current. So by definition, j squared equals negative one, and that single rule is the engine behind everything else in this section.

A complex number combines a real part and this new imaginary part into one object, written as z = a + jb, where a and b are ordinary real numbers. This is called rectangular form: a tells you how far along the "real axis" you are, and b tells you how far along the "imaginary axis" you are, so you can picture z as a point (or an arrow from the origin) on a two-dimensional plane rather than a single point on a number line. That arrow has a length and a direction, which gives you a second way to describe the same number: polar form. The length, called the magnitude, is found with the Pythagorean theorem, |z| = sqrt(a² + b²), and the direction, called the angle or phase, is θ = atan2(b, a) ,  the angle the arrow makes with the positive real axis. Rectangular and polar forms describe the identical number; you switch between them depending on which operation you need to do.

Adding or subtracting complex numbers is easiest in rectangular form: you just add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together, the same way you'd add coordinates. Multiplying is easiest in polar form: you multiply the magnitudes and add the angles. You can also multiply directly in rectangular form by treating j like an unknown and expanding normally, then simplifying using j² = -1 whenever it appears.

Try a concrete pair: z1 = 3 + j4 and z2 = 2 − j2. In rectangular form, z1 + z2 = 5 + j2 ,  just combine real and imaginary parts separately. To multiply, expand the product term by term: (3 + j4)(2 − j2) = 6 − j6 + j8 − j²8. Since j² = -1, that last term becomes +8, so the result is 14 + j2. Now check this against polar form: z1 has magnitude sqrt(3² + 4²) = 5 and angle atan2(4,3) ≈ 53.13°; z2 has magnitude sqrt(2² + 2²) ≈ 2.828 and angle ≈ -45°. Multiplying magnitudes gives 5 × 2.828 ≈ 14.14, and adding angles gives 53.13° − 45° = 8.13°. Converting 14 + j2 back to polar form gives magnitude sqrt(14² + 2²) = sqrt(200) ≈ 14.14 and angle atan2(2,14) ≈ 8.13° ,  the two methods agree, as they must, because they're just two views of the same arithmetic.

Right now this may look like pure algebra with no circuit in sight, but hold onto it: once you start describing voltages and currents that oscillate sinusoidally, you'll represent each signal's amplitude and timing as one complex number, and the addition and multiplication rules you just practiced will become the actual mechanics of analyzing AC circuits.
